summary: At 502 square miles, Los Angeles is physically larger than the entire nation of Tonga, stretching from Pacific surf breaks to the foot of the San Gabriel Mountains — and that sheer sprawl means the "city" contains alpine-adjacent neighborhoods at 1,500 feet of elevation and flat coastal plains practically at sea level, often separated by canyons that make two points five miles apart a twenty-minute drive. The median home value of roughly $879,500 against a median household income of about $80,400 yields a price-to-income ratio near 11:1, meaning even a dual-income household at the median would be stretching hard to buy; median rent at $1,879 consumes about 28 percent of gross monthly income, which partly explains why the city functions simultaneously as a job center — anchored by entertainment, healthcare systems like Kaiser and Cedars-Sinai, aerospace-defense firms, the port complex at San Pedro, and two major university clusters — and a place where long cross-city commutes are routine because housing and employment rarely align in the same corridor. Daily highs average 75°F with nearly ten hours of sunshine year-round, and Griffith Park alone offers over 4,200 acres of trails within city limits. The defining tension is that almost everything you'd want exists somewhere inside the city boundary — the tradeoff is that getting between those things is its own daily negotiation.
